changes.before:
The variance follows directly from the first two factorial moments. Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$,

$$
\mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda.
$$
changes.after:
::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: why a Poisson count has variance equal to its mean"}

The variance follows directly from the first two factorial moments. Summing $k\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda$. Likewise, summing $k(k-1)\Pr(K=k)$ gives $\lambda^2$. Since $K^2=K(K-1)+K$,

$$
\mathbb E[K^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(K)=\mathbb E[K^2]-\mathbb E[K]^2=\lambda.
$$

:::
changes.reason: Mean and variance are already visible. This proof checks those identities without supplying a later prerequisite.

changes.before:
Let $p(\theta,t)$ be the density of the memory coordinate across repeated trials initialized at $\Theta$. The [**Itô convention**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} evaluates a state-dependent noise coefficient at the beginning of each increment. To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta]
&=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta]
+\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\
&=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt).
\end{aligned}
$$

The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta
=\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta.
$$

Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, the density obeys the [**Fokker Planck equation**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}:

::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: from random increments to the memory density equation"}

To pass from random increments to a density equation, choose any smooth function $F(\theta)$. In a short interval $dt$, the zero-drift Itô increment has conditional mean zero and conditional second moment $2D(\theta)dt$. Taylor expansion at the starting coordinate gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E[F(\theta+d\theta)-F(\theta)\mid\theta]
&=F'(\theta)\mathbb E[d\theta\mid\theta]
+\tfrac12F''(\theta)\mathbb E[(d\theta)^2\mid\theta]+o(dt)\\
&=D(\theta)F''(\theta)dt+o(dt).
\end{aligned}
$$

The higher-order terms vanish faster than $dt$ in this diffusion approximation. Averaging over the starting-coordinate density and dividing by $dt$ gives

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int F(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta
=\int F''(\theta)D(\theta)p(\theta,t)\,d\theta.
$$

Take $F$ to vanish outside an interior region, or use boundaries for which the integration terms vanish. Integrating by parts twice moves both derivatives from $F$ onto the product $Dp$. Because the resulting identity holds for every such smooth $F$, it gives the Fokker Planck equation shown above.

:::

chapter_id: ch:MEMORY-DYNAMICS
part_id: part:MECHANISMS
title: How spiking noise moves a stored memory
purpose: A network can keep firing after a stimulus disappears and still lose the value
  that the stimulus supplied. The important question is whether the activity pattern stays
  in the right place, not just whether activity continues. Burak and Fiete study this
  distinction in a network whose stable activity patterns form a continuous set. This
  chapter derives how random spikes move the network along that set. The next chapter
  asks how well another network can read the moving memory.

section_list:
- id: sec:MEMORY-SPIKES
  title: From individual spikes to a slowly changing network state
  summary: How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of
    a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually.
    Incoming activations determine new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those
    activations. This feedback can support activity after the external stimulus has ended.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-LINEARIZATION
  title: Which part of a perturbation survives?
  summary: 'A spike perturbs many aspects of a network''s state. Most of those changes
    decay as the state returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the
    one change that survives: the displacement to a different fixed point.'
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-DIFFUSION
  title: Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
  summary: We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable
    components have relaxed. Multiply the linear stochastic equation by $\mathbf v^T$.
    Since $\mathbf v^TK=0$,
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-SYMMETRIC
  title: Symmetric weights make the projection measurable
  summary: The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. When
    $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$, can we write it using tuning curves and the input to rate rule?
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME
  title: From local spreading to long delay errors
  summary: A local diffusion coefficient answers how variance initially grows. It does
    not by itself say that variance grows at the same rate forever. Boundaries and variation
    of $D$ can change the long time behavior.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE
  title: Random drift, systematic drift, and a mistuned network
  summary: Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original
    value. That random spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction.
    Both can occur, and the derivation of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-FIGURES
  title: Reading the first two figures
  summary: Figure 1A, p. 2 shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green
    point off the attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This
    endpoint defines the instantaneous attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat
    that flow. The difference between the two endpoints is the retained memory change.
    The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the tilted two variable example above.
  level: 2

  summary: How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this
    model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Incoming activations determine
    new firing rates; the resulting spikes renew those activations. This feedback can support activity
    after the external stimulus has ended.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-LINEARIZATION
  title: The network's return flow determines the lasting memory change
  summary: 'A spike perturbs many aspects of a network''s state. Most of those changes decay as the state
    returns to the attractor. To calculate memory loss, we need the one change that survives: the displacement
    to a different fixed point.'
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-DIFFUSION
  title: Projecting spike fluctuations gives the diffusion coefficient
  summary: We can now calculate how much random displacement remains after the stable components have
    relaxed. Multiply the linear stochastic equation by $\mathbf v^T$. Since $\mathbf v^TK=0$,
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-SYMMETRIC
  title: Symmetric weights express diffusion through tuning curves
  summary: The general formula requires the left vector of the network dynamics. When $W_{ij}=W_{ji}$,
    can we write it using tuning curves and the input to rate rule?
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-LONG-TIME
  title: Long delay errors depend on boundaries and local diffusion
  summary: A local diffusion coefficient answers how variance initially grows. It does not by itself say
    that variance grows at the same rate forever. Boundaries and variation of $D$ can change the long
    time behavior.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-DRIFT-SCOPE
  title: A diffusion calculation does not determine systematic drift
  summary: Repeated trials can spread apart even if their average stays at the original value. That random
    spreading differs from a reproducible movement in one direction. Both can occur, and the derivation
    of $D$ alone does not settle the second question.
  level: 2
- id: sec:MEMORY-FIGURES
  title: Figures distinguish memory motion from readout error and test diffusion
  summary: Figure 1A, p. 2 shows the definition of the memory coordinate. Start at a green point off the
    attractor and follow the noise free flow to the black point on it. This endpoint defines the instantaneous
    attractor state. After one noisy interval, repeat that flow. The difference between the two endpoints
    is the retained memory change. The relevant projection follows the flow, as in the tilted two variable
    example above.
  level: 2

  caption: Original guide construction of the tilted decay example, with dimensionless coordinates and
    $a/\lambda=1/2$. After an imposed jump from $(0,0)$ to $(0,2)$, the state relaxes toward $(1,0)$;
    successive time marks crowd toward that endpoint. This illustrates the left and right zero vector
    construction in Burak and Fiete (2012), Supporting Text, Section II, pp. 3–4, Eqs. S10–S16; it is

    is followed by a straight tilted flow toward one zero. Equal time marks crowd toward the endpoint.
    Perpendicular projection would return to zero zero and miss the lasting shift of one. The tangent
    is one zero; the left vector measures delta x plus one half delta y.

- id: fig:MEMORY-SPIKE-TRACE
  kind: figure
  placement: sec:MEMORY-SPIKES
  asset: assets/approved/visuals/memory-spike-trace.png
  caption: Each spike adds one activation unit, which then decays with a 50 ms time constant. Closely
    spaced spikes add to the activation left by earlier spikes. The five spike times are an illustrative
    input, and the activation is calculated exactly from the chapter equation.
  alt: Five spike marks share a time axis with an activation trace. Each mark aligns with a vertical rise
    of one activation unit. The activation decays smoothly between spikes, and nearby spikes build on
    the remaining activation.
  width_inches: 7.29167
  html_fold: never

  kind: figure
  placement: sec:MEMORY-SYMMETRIC
  asset: assets/approved/visuals/memory-inhibition-rates.png
  caption: For the chapter’s two mutually inhibiting cells, b = 20 activation units and tau = 0.1 s give
    opposite changes in the two rates. Their sum remains 200 spikes/s, so local D remains 100 coordinate
    units squared/s. Open endpoints mark the excluded boundaries; the linear interior model does not determine
    boundary behavior. These curves are calculated examples, not simulation data.
  alt: As theta increases through the interior from minus 20 to 20 activation units, r1 increases toward
    200 spikes per second and r2 decreases toward zero. Their dashed sum stays at 200. A lower aligned
    plot shows D constant at 100 coordinate units squared per second. Open endpoint circles exclude both
    boundaries.
  width_inches: 7.29167

  caption: With the same constant D = 0.5 rad²/s, wrapped Gaussian error densities widen toward 1/(2π).
